On SafeWorld, its responses reflect the reference norms more often (Coverage) and more precisely (Faithfulness), exceeding Responder SFT by 18.0 and 14.1 percentage points, respectively. Direct norm evaluation also shows higher norm quality than the base and few-shot generators. The same trained generator improves cultural alignment on SafeWorld across fourteen frozen LLMs spanning five families and 0.8B to 27B parameters, with the largest gains for the smallest models.

Computation and Language.title: AVA-Encoder: Learning to Represent Videos via Reconstruction-Driven Agentic Self-Evolution
Computation and Language.summary: Agentic video creation systems remain far from cinematic-grade quality: their underlying models struggle to plan how story, characters, visuals, and sound fit together, and high-quality creation trajectories to learn such planning abilities are scarce. Finished human films embody this knowledge, but in a tightly coupled audiovisual form that agents cannot directly read or manipulate. We propose the Agentic Video "Auto-Encoder" (AVA-Encoder), which works backward from human films, turning them into agent-native video representations with reconstruction itself as the sole supervision. It encodes a film into a Film Knowledge Graph (Film KG) of structured-text nodes, typed dependency edges, and linked multimodal assets, then regenerates the film from this graph with a fixed decoder. Crucially, by distilling reconstruction residuals into textual gradients, AVA-Encoder drives a dual-loop self-evolution: an outer loop autonomously discovers a generalizable encoding strategy entirely from unlabeled videos, while an inner loop refines each video's Film KG at test time. AVA-Encoder improves reconstruction fidelity by 20.9 percentage points over the strongest baseline, and its autonomously learned strategy outperforms a human-tuned strategy using 70% fewer prompt tokens. Our representations drive three downstream breakthroughs: (1) Film KGs enable coordinated graph-based editing and (2) improve one-shot video generation across four open-source frameworks, while (3) fine-tuning agents on our reverse-engineered trajectories boosts video creation quality by 38.7%. We release the framework and a dataset of 500 Film KGs with over 27,000 creation trajectories.

Computation and Language.title: Sports Agent: A Self-Evolving System for Conversational Data Analytics
Computation and Language.summary:
Conversational sports analytics requires accurate, evidence-based responses with low latency. Changes in query distributions, data resources, and model behavior can degrade static agent configurations, motivating controlled evolution guided by runtime evidence.
  We present Sports Agent, a self-evolving framework integrating an Agentic SQL Model for structured-data reasoning, a harness for planning and tool orchestration, and a unified Feedback Engine connecting online execution with offline evolution. The engine assesses responses and execution trajectories, verifies factual claims, diagnoses failures, and generates evolution signals. Model evolution combines SQL-to-Question Scaling for coverage expansion with Graph-Guided Scaling for error-targeted synthesis. Generated questions undergo trajectory distillation and quality filtering for iterative supervised fine-tuning, followed by a separate Post-RL stage. Harness evolution translates recurrent failures into bounded prompt and skill updates, validated through independent audits, execution replay, and regression testing. Performance-tolerance checks guard against unacceptable degradation during simplification.
  The resulting Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-based model outperforms Qwen3.8-Max on sports question answering and analysis while achieving approximately three times the inference efficiency. Across 30 harness-evolution rounds, the aggregate performance score improves by 10.8 points. In a live sports analytics product, the evolved system improves factual correctness by 10.5 points and average response length, a proxy for answer richness, by 158.1%, while reducing average latency by 41.3% relative to the baseline.

Computation and Language.title: Rethinking Sequential Locate-Then-Edit: Optimality and Stability
Computation and Language.summary: The Locate-Then-Edit framework enables efficient knowledge updates in large language models without requiring full retraining. Recent research has increasingly focused on sequential editing, where knowledge arrives continuously and the model is updated incrementally. However, existing sequential methods commonly suffer from catastrophic forgetting and model collapse after only a few hundred edits. In contrast, batch editing - which jointly optimizes all edits and yields the optimal solution under a specified editing objective - can support tens of thousands of edits with high edit efficacy while preserving the model's general capabilities, resulting in a substantial performance gap between the two editing paradigms. In this paper, we demonstrate that this gap can be closed via a batch-equivalent sequential editing approach. Moreover, we investigate the underlying mechanism of model degradation in existing sequential methods by analyzing the convergence behavior of weight perturbations as edits accumulate. Our analysis reveals that current methods typically exhibit linear or logarithmic growth in perturbation, whereas the proposed batch-equivalent method achieves time-invariant growth, thereby theoretically guaranteeing long-term stability and preserving the integrity of pretrained knowledge throughout massive-scale sequential editing.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted by NeurIPS 2026. 10 pages of main text, 6 figures, and 2 tables. The full manuscript contains 41 pages, including references and supplementary material. This work concerns sequential knowledge editing within the locate-then-edit framework

Computation and Language.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
Computation and Language.summary: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
Computation and Language.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/AfifahK/bias-eval-construct-validity

Computation and Language.title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
Computation and Language.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) show promise for medical education, but most existing systems focus on localized interactions such as question answering or single-turn feedback, rather than organizing an entire clinical case into a decision-centered learning trajectory. We introduce \textit{MedGame}, a framework that transforms static clinical cases into structured, executable storytelling games. MedGame uses a dual-engine design: a Medical Narrative Designer synthesizes case-grounded clinical storylines with states and decision nodes, while a Story Director converts them into dependency-aware multimodal orchestration plans rendered by our released interactive platform. We construct MedGame Bench, a 5,000-case benchmark and evaluation protocol for Medical Narrative Generation and Story Direction. Experiments show that task-specific fine-tuning substantially improves open-source LLMs on MedGame Bench and narrows the gap with commercial models. A pilot student study further shows that learners perceive MedGame as more engaging and useful than text-only alternatives.
Computation and Language.comment: Work in Progress; an explorational design and study on AI+Education+Game. Updated an author's affiliation. A further revision (v3) is in preparation

Computation and Language.title: Can Language Models Learn to Forecast Stock Prices?
Computation and Language.summary: We build BETA, a chronological sandbox over S&P 500 stocks in which a model calls tools to retrieve prices, indicators, and news available up to a decision date, and then forecasts the stock's future return. Evaluating frontier models in this sandbox reveals three systematic weaknesses: their scores decline as the test period approaches the present while a simple momentum baseline stays stable, they predict gains far more often than gains occur, and they predict moves much smaller than those that are realized. We then train models directly in the sandbox. We first fine-tune on filtered, hindsight-generated tool-use trajectories for historical tasks judged predictable from the evidence available at the time, teaching the model how to investigate a stock. We then apply reinforcement learning with rewards based on realized returns. During RL, long investigations frequently exceed the context window. We therefore introduce a selective compaction tool that allows the model to compress chosen portions of its interaction history. We address these challenges with Context-Aligned Turn-Level PPO, which uses a turn-level critic and computes policy updates using each turn's actual context. The resulting models, which we call AURA, substantially reduce all three weaknesses. Training improves the 8B model's score from 24.0 to 47.0 and the 30B model's from 27.4 to 54.7, with the latter surpassing all evaluated frontier models on our benchmark and achieving its largest margin on the most recent test period. These scores describe tasks selected for alignment between the available evidence and the realized return. Across all 412 candidates in the latest period, the trained 30B model still leads (35.17), while the trained 8B model scores below momentum (25.91 versus 28.33).

Computation and Language.title: Rethinking Knowledge Distillation for Diffusion Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: Knowledge distillation has recently proven highly effective for improving autoregressive models, but its applicability to DLMs remains poorly understood. We present the first systematic study of KD for DLMs and uncover two non-intuitive failures of classical forward-KL (FKL) distillation: (i) student perplexity does not improve monotonically with more teacher-generated data, and (ii) on the same teacher-generated corpus, FKL distillation underperforms simply training the student with the original DLM denoising objective. To address them, we propose a unified, data-free distillation framework for masked DLMs. First, the framework runs an off-policy distillation phase that absorbs general knowledge from a static set of teacher-generated data. Then, the framework employs on-policy distillation which consists of three techniques: a trajectory loss along the student's own reverse process, confidence reweighting that down-weights tokens where the teacher is unsure, and a trust-region anchor that stabilizes the moving target. On MDLM, the resulting student attains a GPT-2 perplexity of $24.75$, surpassing the teacher's $27.04$; on Dream-7B distillation to a 93M student model, the framework reduces Qwen-2.5 perplexity from the FKL-distilled baseline of $25.23$ to $19.83$ while preserving performance on zero-shot general capability benchmarks.

Computation and Language.title: Verifiable but Not Predictable: What Sentence Embeddings Know About Propositional Decomposition
Computation and Language.summary: Quality control for proposition decomposition by large language models (LLMs) raises two asymmetric questions. After decomposition, one can verify: given a sentence and a candidate proposition, does the proposition belong to that sentence? Before decomposition, one would like to predict: how many propositions should the sentence yield? On PropSegmEnt, a corpus of English Wikipedia sentences each segmented by three human annotators, we find that the two questions live in different representational spaces. A natural language inference (NLI) judge verifies membership with 92.8% accuracy and an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.977, and its residual errors turn out to be mostly propositions that are true in document context rather than genuine entailment mistakes. Vector geometry cannot verify: cosine similarity saturates, and a sentence embedding is not a linear combination of its propositions' embeddings. For prediction, every symbolic anchor we test, namely token count, the CPIDR idea-density counter, and a Neo-Davidsonian predicate count, reduces to a length proxy once token count is controlled. A linear ridge probe on sentence embeddings is the only predictor that keeps genuine count signal: its length-partialled correlation with human counts is 0.40-0.49 with bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs) excluding zero, and it orders length-matched sentence pairs correctly 67-71% of the time against a 50% chance level, statistically matching the inter-annotator agreement ceiling. This signal survives INT8 quantization without loss, INT4 at a small cost, and Matryoshka truncation to 256 dimensions, and it works as well in a 2021 encoder as in a 2025 one. Its structured weakness is a systematic under-splitting of long sentences. We distill the protocol lessons, including a retracted pilot study, into a checklist for probing length-confounded quantities.

Computation and Language.title: Luxical: High-Speed Lexical-Dense Text Embeddings
Computation and Language.summary: Frontier language model quality increasingly hinges on our ability to organize web-scale text corpora for training. Today's dominant tools trade off speed and flexibility: lexical classifiers (e.g., FastText) are fast but limited to producing classification output scores, while the vector-valued outputs of transformer text embedding models flexibly support numerous workflows (e.g., clustering, classification, and retrieval) but are computationally expensive to produce. We introduce Luxical, a library for high-speed "lexical-dense" text embeddings that aims to recover the best properties of both approaches for web-scale text organization. Luxical combines sparse TF--IDF features, a small ReLU network, and a knowledge distillation training regimen to approximate large transformer embedding models at a fraction of their operational cost. In this technical report, we describe the Luxical architecture and training objective and evaluate a concrete Luxical model in two disparate applications: a targeted webcrawl document retrieval test and an end-to-end language model data curation task grounded in text classification. In these tasks we demonstrate speedups ranging from 3x to 100x over varying-sized neural baselines, and comparable to FastText model inference during the data curation task. On these evaluations, the tested Luxical model illustrates favorable compute/quality trade-offs for large-scale text organization, matching the quality of neural baselines. Luxical is available as open-source software at https://github.com/datologyai/luxical.
Computation and Language.comment: 9 pages, 6 figures. v2 fixes typos only. v3 corrects Luxical-One first-layer projection width typo (92 -> 96) and minor typographical errors

Computation and Language.title: Sparse-to-Sparse Feature Learning for Cross-Layer Analysis and Steering
Computation and Language.summary: Understanding how models internally represent information is a central challenge in interpretation and control. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) decompose dense hidden representations into sparse features, and cross-layer methods capture structure spanning multiple layers. However, existing objectives do not explicitly train the sparse code at one layer to predict the sparse code at the next layer. We propose sparse-to-sparse feature learning (S2S), where sparse features at each intermediate layer are trained to predict those of the immediately following layer, with the final layer anchored by an output-distribution loss and optimization proceeding sequentially from output to input. Experiments across eight language models show stronger adjacent-layer correspondence than matched sparse-feature baselines. We evaluate feature-based interventions at matched output-distribution shift, separating steering-induced effects from sparse-pathway reconstruction effects. Causal ablation provides complementary evidence beyond correspondence metrics.

Computation and Language.title: A History-Aware Visually Grounded Critic for Computer Use Agents
Computation and Language.summary: Various test-time interventions for Computer Use Agents (CUAs), including critic models, have been developed to improve performance through pre-execution action evaluation in complex Graphical User Interface (GUI) environments. However, existing critics suffer from two key limitations: they (1) focus primarily on short-sighted decision loops (e.g., forgetting earlier actions) and (2) lack the visual grounding needed to detect flawed actions (e.g., clicking wrong UI elements). To address these, we introduce HiViG, a History-aware Visually Grounded test-time framework, built around a multimodal critic trained on real GUI trajectories to abstract past interactions into a compact record and to evaluate actions with visual grounding. At test time, HiViG integrates the critic into the policy decision loop to provide macro-action history, which summarizes the policy's completed achievements, and visually grounded critique, which verifies raw execution coordinates against the current screenshot to intercept errors before execution. Across web, mobile, and desktop benchmarks, HiViG consistently outperforms existing scalar and verbal critics, improving average success rates over the strongest baseline by 5.8% for Qwen3-VL-32B and 9.0% for Gemini-3-Flash, and demonstrates strong cross-platform generalization. Ablations show that macro-action history mitigates short-sighted planning and visually grounded critique reduces execution errors, with both components being critical for test-time scaling in long-horizon GUI tasks.

Computation and Language.title: State Space Attention: Learning Context-Dependent Memory Retention
Computation and Language.summary: Standard attention's key-value cache grows linearly with context length. Bounding it raises the question of what a sequence model should retain for long-context reasoning. We argue this choice should be learned, and introduce State Space Attention (SSA), which learns to keep a bounded set of past representations and reads them with standard attention. A learned scorer rescores every chunk against newly arriving context and the rest of memory. A fixed-context Transformer is then the special case that always keeps the most recent tokens. We train the scorer and reader jointly, either moving gradually from a differentiable soft weighting of memories to hard retention, or with hard retention from the start. To produce signal for the scorer, we generate supervised samples during training, a technique we call recovery. We compare SSA with recurrent models, bounded-memory attention methods, and full-attention Transformers across retrieval, variable tracking, multi-hop reasoning, and language modeling. On our retrieval and reasoning benchmarks, SSA matches or comes within a few points of full attention on most tasks, far outperforms a Transformer with the same readable budget on every long-context retrieval task we evaluate, and matches or outperforms one with about 4 times that budget, while using constant inference memory. The largest remaining gap to full attention at small language model scale is on RULER. SSA makes a fixed number of tokens useful over a longer context, and since it reads memory with standard attention, we propose that it can be stacked with KV cache eviction methods. We also pretrain and post-train 400M-parameter models and measure how SSA's training and inference costs scale with context length and model size. Together, these experiments examine the capabilities and limitations of learned memory retention for long-context sequence modeling.

Computation and Language.title: Failure Broadens, Success Sharpens: Continual Adaptation of Tool-Use Agents Across Diverse Tasks with Dual-Polarity Memory
Computation and Language.summary: Large language model agents can self-improve over time by utilizing procedural memory derived from prior task trajectories, yet the distinct utilities of memories derived from local successes and failures remain underexplored. This work studies this question in a realistic setting with heterogeneous streams of multi-domain tool-use tasks and various environment constraints common in real-world scenarios. We develop \emph{Dual-Polarity Memory with Periodic Maintenance} (DualPM), a simple, retrieval-free memory workflow characterized by (1) customizable reflection and procedural memory generation from both local successes and failures within each trajectory, and (2) periodic memory consolidation over long task streams under a given memory capacity, preventing memory explosion. Online prequential evaluation with fine-grained metrics reveals that failure memory more strongly broadens coverage, success memory better streamlines execution, while combining both polarities effectively integrates both benefits. Further studies demonstrate that DualPM enables cross-domain memory generalization and continual memory adaptation, while external evaluation on EvoMemBench reveals the portability and effectiveness of DualPM as a general long-term procedural memory method.
Computation and Language.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 Workshop: Towards Test-Time Continual Learning Agents

Computation and Language.title: Aligned Machine: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multimodal Embedding Similarity via Human Comparative Judgements
Computation and Language.summary: Embedding models increasingly inform how people search, recommend, and retrieve information, yet we lack credible ways to test whether these similarity judgments reflect how humans understand meaning. Existing benchmarks typically rely on static, expert-labeled pairs with coarse Likert-style annotations, limiting scalability and making it difficult to obtain consistent, high-confidence annotations. We introduce Aligned Machine, an interactive, public-facing platform that transforms broad participation into a continuously growing Human-Aligned Similarity Benchmark (HASB) for evaluating semantic alignment in embedding-based systems. Participants complete a cognitively-natural, forced-choice task, comparing two pairs of items (text or images) and selecting which pair is more similar. This comparative design is accessible to non-experts, yields clean preference data, and supports robust aggregation. We report results from an initial deployment with 115 participants contributing 2,875 total labeled pairs and 872 unique pairs. Using HASB, we evaluated 12 widely used embedding models and found only partial alignment between embedding similarity and human judgments. Text-only models consistently achieve higher overall agreement than multimodal models, while multimodal performance varies systematically by task type: alignment is strongest for image-image comparisons, weaker for image-text comparisons, and lowest for text-text comparisons. Aligned Machine is designed to evolve over time as participation grows, supporting longitudinal analysis, domain-specific studies, bias detection, and measurement of concept drift across model versions. By combining accessible public participation with rigorous comparative evaluation, HASB provides a scalable and accountable framework for auditing semantic alignment in embedding models.

Computation and Language.title: SEEL: Towards End-to-End 3D Sign Generation with Language Models
Computation and Language.summary: 3D sign language generation aims to produce signing motion from written text. Motivated by the linguistic nature of sign language, recent methods combine a motion tokenizer with a language model to predict motion tokens from text. However, both components are optimized through a two-stage pipeline with mismatched objectives: the tokenizer minimizes reconstruction error in isolation, while the generator learns from rigid one-hot reference tokens. A straightforward end-to-end extension bridges discrete token selection with straight-through estimators (STE), suffering from biased gradients and codebook collapse. To address these limitations, we propose SEEL, an end-to-end framework that aligns tokenization and generation with motion quality through two complementary mechanisms. First, to overcome rigid one-hot supervision, reconstruction-aware generation decodes candidate tokens in context and converts their 3D motion errors into soft targets, guiding the generator with physical motion quality. Second, to propagate generation feedback without STE, generation-aware tokenization passes continuous codebook expectations through the frozen generator, routing generated-motion gradients to the tokenizer to prevent codebook collapse. Combining both mechanisms enables the tokenizer and generator to co-evolve, achieving state-of-the-art performance on CSL-Daily, How2Sign, and Phoenix-2014T. Code and models will be released to facilitate future research.

Computation and Language.title: PeerReveal: Learning to Generalize in AI Peer Review Detection
Computation and Language.summary: Can we distinguish fully AI-generated reviews from those using AI only to rewrite human judgement? Furthermore, can we do so reliably when reviews are generated from diverse AI models and workflows across scientific domains? To this end, we introduce PeerReveal, a new detector that grounds its decisions in learned relationships between a review's claims and reference claims drawn from AI-generated reviews of the same paper, complemented by review-level textual signals. We evaluate PeerReveal on PeerShift, a new, challenging test set of 5,430 reviews spanning multiple domains, including machine learning, life sciences, and social sciences, combining variation in disciplinary review conventions with diverse AI review-production mechanisms. With regular training, PeerReveal achieves 70.52% pooled Macro-F1 on this benchmark, improving over the strongest baseline by 11.48 points. We develop an effective and practical adversarial training framework that further improves the detector's generalization using a small local generator optimized to produce challenging reviews, raising pooled Macro-F1 from 70.52% to 82.40%. These results show that robust AI-review detection benefits from richer review-level evidence and adversarial training on more challenging generation processes.

Computers and Society.title: A Survey of Security, Privacy, and Ethics of Large Language Models in Telecom
Computers and Society.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into telecommunications for customer service, network analytics, and operational support. While offering efficiency and innovation, their deployment raises critical privacy, security, and ethical challenges due to the uniquely sensitive and longitudinal nature of telecom data. This paper presents a survey of LLM risks and safeguards in telecom context. Our survey introduces a telecom-specific taxonomy linking privacy, security, and ethics with use cases and outlines open research challenges such as longitudinal data privacy, cross-border compliance, and scalable guardrails.
Computers and Society.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, published in COMSNETS 2025 conference

Computers and Society.title: Model Weights, Airlocks and Sandboxes: A Call for Technical Validation of Re-identification Tests under the EDPB Anonymisation Guidelines
Computers and Society.summary: The Guidelines 02/2026 on anonymisation of the European Data Protection Board (EDPB), published for consultation in July 2026, assess anonymity relative to the entities that may access data. They bring AI models into scope and call for testing, but do not say how a re-identification test should be designed or validated, or how far its result counts as evidence. Building on our reply to the consultation, we describe a framework based on a secure processing environment whose outputs are reviewed before release (an airlock), and distinguish forms of release and three types of evidence: formal, empirical and indirect. We raise seven open questions, each with a scenario, and examine their technical side in three settings: the release of model weights (the trained parameters of a machine learning model), review at an airlock, and regulatory sandboxes, in which an authority supervises development and testing. In each setting the assessment depends on how far a test result can be relied on, since a failed re-identification attempt may mean only that the test was too weak. Drawing on measurement practice in other regulated fields, we call for re-identification tests to be validated as measurement methods, with stated detection limit, bias and uncertainty.
Computers and Society.comment: 52 pages, 2 figures, 4 tables. Extended version of a paper submitted to the Privacy Symposium 2027: the 15-page body is unchanged, and 30 pages of appendices are added

Computers and Society.title: Proverbs As A Window On Collective Prescriptions
Computers and Society.summary: Proverbs, as repositories of traditional wisdom, have informed human reasoning for millennia. Yet the collective prescriptions they encode have remained largely unquantified. We introduce a computational framework to analyze nearly 50,000 English-language proverbs. Using large language models, validated against human judgments, we map the topical landscape of proverbs, assess their prescriptive power, and quantify their recommendations on key dimensions of human judgment and behavior. We find that most proverbs are prescriptive, offering guidance in domains under individual control, such as preparation and prudent action, whereas proverbs about uncontrollable circumstances, such as fate and mortality, tend to describe rather than prescribe. When prescriptive proverbs take a consistent stance, they favor caution over risk, long-term over short-term outcomes, honesty over deception, and kindness over malice, and show a moderate tendency toward suspicion over trust. On dimensions involving genuine trade-offs, especially autonomy versus compliance, proverbs provide contradicting advice rather than a single recommendation. This analysis provides a quantitative map of the collective prescriptions in a culture's proverbial wisdom, revealing a core of prudent, honest, and forward-looking guidance alongside varied advice where circumstances dictate the best course of action.

Computers and Society.title: Inferential Privacy Leakage in Anonymized Conversational AI Logs
Computers and Society.summary: Conversations with ChatGPT have become a new kind of personal record: long, accumulated over months, and routinely touching health, work, family, and belief in ways search queries never did. These logs now reach many parties beyond the platform. They are shared with researchers, released as public datasets, retained under court order, and prepared for advertising, usually after names, places, and explicit identifiers have been removed, on the assumption that what remains is safe to hold and share. We test that assumption with complete ChatGPT histories donated, with consent, by 1,057 users in Brazil, India, Nigeria, and Pakistan, each paired with self-reported demographics, and for 212 of them with their Google Search and YouTube histories as well. Users volunteer personal information constantly: 34.5% of 1.24 million messages contain it, and the median user does so within the first 14% of their history. We then remove messages flagged for explicit demographic self-identification and ask an open-weights LLM to infer each user's age bracket, gender, and country from the remaining history. It recovers country at weighted F1 0.86, gender at 0.76, and age bracket at 0.51, well above majority-class and feature-based baselines, with most of the gender and country signal already present in the first 5% of a history. Redaction removes what users say about themselves but it does not remove what the model assumes about them. The same users' search and watch histories show ChatGPT to be a comparable profiling surface, not a redundant one. We draw out what this means for the inference criterion in anonymization standards, for research data releases, and for who bears the cost when a model trained on someone else's defaults fills in the blanks.

Computers and Society.title: Decision and Support Mechanisms under Platform Information Overload: A Generative-Agent Experiment on College Application
Computers and Society.summary:
People now make major personal decisions surrounded by far more online information than they can read, yet research says little about why information overload affects some people more than others. We study this question in Chinese college applications, a high-stakes decision made amid heavy online content where each list can be scored objectively once admission cutoffs are released.
  We simulated 90 applicants using language-model agents with family backgrounds from a national household survey. Each applicant wrote a list of eight programs alone and revised it four times: after parent and teacher advice, after reading a feed of twenty real online items, after a mentor gave advice based on the applicant's rank, and after a second mentor offered only emotional support. After each step, we scored the list and asked how anxious the applicant felt.
  When applicants decided alone, admission rates were similar across socioeconomic status (SES) groups. The gap appeared once family background entered through parents and teachers: low-SES parents asked for low tuition and schools near home, leaving fewer reachable programs, so admission was 100% for high-SES vs. 77% for low-SES applicants. The platform feed gave everyone the same amount of information but did not narrow this gap; applicants maintained their decisions while reporting higher anxiety. Personalized advice cut the gap to 3 points by raising low-SES admission from 80% to 97%, but led students to higher tuition and less preferred majors. Emotional support did not further lower anxiety, but helped applicants go back and use helpful items they had ignored.
  These simulation results suggest that when information is abundant, more of it neither improves decisions nor reduces inequality. Personalized information does both, while moving inequality from the outcome to its cost.

Computers and Society.title: Atunda: Building an Afrogenic Dance Movement Dataset for AI-Driven Classification
Computers and Society.summary: This paper introduces Atunda, the first systematically collected video dataset of Afrogenic dance moves, designed for training and evaluating deep learning models for movement classification. The first phase of the dataset includes nearly 400 videos covering 13 distinct dance moves from African and African Diaspora performative culture, making it the first AI-ready resource of its kind. Using this dataset, we train and evaluate various configurations of temporal convolutional neural networks, achieving a classification accuracy exceeding 95%. The baseline results provide a benchmark for future studies in movement classification, especially in the understudied area of Afrogenic performative culture and tradition. This work lays the foundation for developing in the future digital metrics of similarity, automated attribution systems, and tools that preserve and promote the cultural heritage of Afrogenic dances.

Computers and Society.title: Where Does the Asymmetry Enter? Staging a Fairness Audit Across a Fused Multimodal Moderation Pipeline
Computers and Society.summary: Almost every short-video upload now passes through a classifier that fuses video, speech, and on-screen text into one decision about whether it may be seen. It moderates every language community on the platform at once, and fairness across them is judged, if at all, from one accuracy score. That score is compatible with error falling almost entirely on one language group. An audit that goes looking reads the model's decisions, the last stage of a long pipeline and the one whose test has the fewest items. We ask where in a fused pipeline a subgroup asymmetry can be detected at all: in what the classifier may read, in what its branches encode, or in what it decides. We answer this with a post-hoc audit of a published TikTok classifier, holding all three stages to one significance standard using only its logged decisions, labels, and pre-fusion features, with source language as the subgroup axis. The asymmetry is significant at the stage deciding what the model may read, and again in what the text branch encodes. At the earlier stage, a language-blind cap admits less of a Vietnamese clip than an English one, for reasons of segmentation, not verbosity. The asymmetry is undetectable at the decision, where the smallest subgroup leaves twelve items to test. An audit reading only decisions looks where its evidence is thinnest; the same test staged upstream recovers a disparity the decision-level view returns as noise.
Computers and Society.comment: Accepted at the 40th Pacific Asia Conference on Language, Information and Computation (PACLIC 40)

Computers and Society.title: Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting: Practical insights from needs, implementations, and governance across Dutch institutions
Computers and Society.summary: Academic LLM hosting is emerging as an operational infrastructure domain with recurring socio-technical patterns, tensions, and governance requirements across institutions. Based on a workshop with academic infrastructure, research-support, education, and policy-adjacent stakeholders, this paper synthesizes current practices and open questions around institutionally governed LLM services for Dutch academia. It highlights challenges around deployment models, energy and utilization, governance, tooling, commercial integration, and research and education use cases, and identifies emerging directions for service pathways, coordination, and responsible operation.
authors: the Towards Democratized Academic LLM Hosting Workshop Consortium

Computers and Society.title: The cost of being seen as AI in group bargaining
Computers and Society.summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in collective decision-making, people's perceptions of AI may shape who reaches agreement and what they receive. We studied this in a repeated three-player majoritarian bargaining game with 2,234 participants. Players saw each opponent identified as Human or AI. The instructions described AI as acting either independently or on behalf of a human. Human participants made every decision. In mixed groups, players presented as AI received fewer points in opening offers, were included in fewer final agreements and earned about 18% less per round than those presented as Human. Smaller payoffs in agreements that included them accounted for most of the observed gap. Further analysis found a payoff gap even when all three players agreed. Social perceptions of AI may therefore shape who benefits from collective decisions, with potential costs for people represented by AI.
Computers and Society.comment: Under review, main manuscript and supplementary materials

Computers and Society.title: Data Centers: The Error of Generalizing Environmental and Socioeconomic Impacts. The Need for a Contextualized Assessment of Computing Infrastructure in Brazil and Worldwide
Computers and Society.summary: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence and cloud computing has intensified debates about the environmental and socioeconomic impacts of data centers, including electricity and water consumption, noise, land use, and employment. A recurring methodological problem in these debates is the use of global data, or of evidence produced in a particular country, to draw conclusions about facilities located in very different settings. This paper argues that the impacts of a data center depend on the geographic, climatic, energy, technological, economic, and regulatory conditions of the territory where it operates, and must therefore be assessed at the appropriate territorial and technological scale. Using Brazil as a case, we discuss the country's predominantly renewable electricity mix and the curtailment of renewable generation, the reported prevalence of closed-loop cooling, national and municipal noise regulations, the water-efficiency requirement of the new Redata tax regime, and the ongoing litigation over the Pec{é}m data center in the state of Cear{á}. We also examine a recent study of data centers in Northern Virginia, showing the limits of its external validity and of its noise measurements. We propose a multiscale assessment framework and conclude that international evidence should inform which questions are asked, not predetermine the answers -- a principle that applies equally to claims of harm and to claims of safety.

Computers and Society.title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
Computers and Society.summary: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.

Computers and Society.title: The Socratic PAUSE: safeguarding scientific judgement at AI speed
Computers and Society.summary: Generative AI can turn a tentative scientific question into hypotheses, methods, code and interpretations within minutes. Yet generating a contribution does not establish that it deserves scientific reliance: researchers must still examine its evidence, assumptions and implications, and remain accountable for the decision to rely on it. Using Einstein's sketch of scientific discovery as a lens, we argue that AI has accelerated discovery far more than justification. In human-AI research partnerships, confidence can therefore outgrow evidence through three mechanisms: recursive reinforcement, loss of provenance and miscalibrated reliance on AI-generated contributions. Verification debt accumulates when such contributions are carried into later claims or decisions without adequate scrutiny. Accordingly, we propose the Socratic Pause as a deliberate checkpoint at consequential decision gates, where an AI contribution remains provisional while a researcher examines its basis. The PAUSE protocol structures this examination through five steps: Pin down the claim, Ask and challenge, Uncover assumptions and alternatives, Scrutinise the evidence and Exercise judgement. It concludes with a recorded decision to accept, revise, reject or defer the contribution. We show how AI research tools can support this practice without displacing human judgement, and outline a framework for evaluating whether it improves verification, decision-making and independent understanding. The aim is to preserve the freedom to explore with AI while ensuring that those responsible for the work can say what was examined, what remains uncertain and why the next step is justified.

Computers and Society.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
Computers and Society.summary: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.

Computers and Society.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
Computers and Society.summary: The bestseller Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and naïve Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

Computers and Society.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
Computers and Society.summary: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.

Computers and Society.title: Silent on Code? A Computing Lens on Generative AI Guidance at Canadian Polytechnics and Research Universities
Computers and Society.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools now write, explain, and debug code, which changes how computing students learn and how their work is assessed. Instructors, however, act within institutional guidance written largely with essays in mind. We report a document analysis of the public, institution-level GenAI guidance of the 13 members of Polytechnics Canada and the 15 members of the U15 Group of Canadian Research Universities, retrieved in October 2026. Using a 27-item codebook spanning governance, integrity and assessment, data and legal issues, values, AI literacy, and a computing lens, we find that both sectors leave course-level decisions to instructors, although polytechnics more often prohibit use unless the instructor permits it (8 of 13 vs. 4 of 14), and converge on disclosure, links to academic integrity policy, and, in most institutions, the expectation that programs adapt rules to their discipline. Polytechnics frame GenAI as workforce preparation substantively far more often (7 of 13 vs. 0 of 14), whereas universities more often address assessment redesign. Twelve of 27 institutions with retrievable guidance mention code, but almost always as one output type among many; none names an AI coding assistant or provides substantive code-specific guidance on attribution, assessment, or licensing. Institution-level guidance is thus not silent on code but leaves programming-specific questions largely to programs and instructors. We propose five elements of discipline-level guidance for computing and release our codebook and coded dataset.
Computers and Society.comment: 5 pages, 1 figure. Accepted at 2027 the 15th International Conference on Information and Education Technology (ICIET)

Computers and Society.title: How AI Is Reconfiguring Work in India: A Task-Based Framework for Understanding Augmentation, Displacement, New Roles and the Changing Structure of Jobs
Computers and Society.summary: Public debate on AI and Indian employment tends to compress a complicated phenomenon into a single binary: will AI take a given job, or not. This paper argues that the accurate picture is a taxonomy rather than a binary. AI rarely replaces a job wholesale; more often it automates a bundle of tasks within a job, and the size of that bundle varies with task structure, sector, regulatory setting, and, distinctively in India's case, the economics of AI access itself. We propose a four-level framework (task, job, occupation, labour-market outcome) and classify Indian job impact into two broad regimes: jobs where AI has automated most of the skill bundle and the human is reduced largely to validation, and jobs where the human remains the primary driver and AI functions as a productivity tool. Each regime splits further into policy-relevant sub-types. Drawing on Indian evidence from business process outsourcing, manufacturing, MSMEs, sanitation, financial services, law, and software engineering, we show that every job in our sample has had to be reimagined, through task-level augmentation, task reallocation, or a genuinely new role built around operating the machine, rather than simply eliminated or defended unchanged. We close with a distributional analysis of who bears the cost of this reimagining and a three-pronged policy recommendation: continue encouraging AI diffusion, invest in India-specific labour-market research, and pair adoption with structured worker-transition pathways.

Computers and Society.title: Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework
Computers and Society.summary: Open-weight models advance transparency, research, and innovation, and spread the benefits of AI more widely. They also carry distinct risks. A release cannot be undone, safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning, and no single party can monitor use or withdraw the model. Managing these risks therefore requires an approach tailored to open release. This framework addresses the governance challenge at the heart of that choice. Co-developed by Concordia AI and Z AI, it adapts the full risk management lifecycle, from risk assessment to mitigation and governance, to the unique properties of open-weight models. This document does not resolve every tension between openness and safety. Rather, it provides the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation for navigating these tensions. As frontier open-weight releases accelerate, risk management best practice and standards are urgently needed. We invite researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society to build on this framework and advance the science and practice of open-weight AI governance.

Computers and Society.title: Language models call themselves AI but do not favor AI over people
Computers and Society.summary: Many fear that AI systems will side with one another against people. Social identity theory, which explains why people favor their own group, offers one way to examine this fear. Seen through this theory, AI would side with AI only if it treated AI as its group and favored AI over people. In three experiments, 24 language models favored a group they were assigned to, even a team of AI agents. With no group assigned, they gave a person more money and credit than an AI agent. Prompts that made them say they belong with AI changed their behavior much less than an assigned team did. These models call themselves AI but do not favor AI over people. Judged by social identity theory, they show no sign of siding with AI against people.
Computers and Society.comment: 42 pages (14 main text, 28 Supplementary Materials), 7 figures

Computers and Society.title: Beyond Disclosure: Compositional Privacy Harm in AI Systems
Computers and Society.summary: Privacy law attaches obligations to each stage of information processing, whether it be collection, use, storage, or disclosure. We examine how legally cognisable privacy harm emerges across this full lifecycle rather than at any single one of these points. We argue that privacy risk in AI systems is compositional, arising from the interaction of memorisation, extraction, inference and contextual transfer. Disclosure is therefore not the sole threshold of privacy harm: legally significant consequences may emerge even where no underlying record is reproduced verbatim. Drawing on contextual integrity, we argue that privacy protection must extend across the lifecycle of AI-mediated information rather than attach to disclosure alone.

Computers and Society.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
Computers and Society.summary: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones, and what becomes of such a gift once it is in use? We present MERIDIAN, a design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town, framed by a birthday prologue and a fictional wedding. This second version extends the record by four weeks. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct seven design changes from 152 commits, 36 changelog versions and four design specifications. In those weeks the site gained three products that are not levels: an infirmary for the days after a quarrel, which began with a remark by the recipient; a page for her booked flight, which replaces a symbolic ticket with a real one; and a request box whose messages are answered, while the designer sleeps, by a pipeline of a local language model and a hosted one. The request box ends the first version's claim of no author-operated backend, and we trace where her files now travel. An audit reproduced 263 passing unit tests; the progress model is unchanged and keeps its exhaustive check of 1,024 codes. The answering pipeline was tested in parts, and it began to receive real requests on the night it was built. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcome is reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs: between authoring a gift and leaving the recipient free to decline or reshape it, and between being reachable across thirteen hours and answering in person. The site is at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.
Computers and Society.comment: 27 pages, 25 figures, 11 tables. v2 adds four weeks of record and describes the dashboard, three further products, server, automated answering pipeline, service worker, and pose-analysis program. It corrects the backend claim and updates the audit. See "Changes in Version 2". Design case with no recipient evaluation reported

Computers and Society.title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
Computers and Society.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current LLMs remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.

Computers and Society.title: The WMDP Benchmark: Measuring and Reducing Malicious Use With Unlearning
Computers and Society.summary: The White House AI Action Plan highlights the risks of large language models (LLMs) empowering malicious actors in developing biological, cyber, and chemical weapons. To measure these risks, government institutions and major AI labs are developing evaluations for hazardous capabilities in LLMs. However, current evaluations are private, preventing further research into mitigating risk. Furthermore, they focus on only a few, highly specific pathways for malicious use. To fill these gaps, we publicly release the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) benchmark, a dataset of 3,668 multiple-choice questions that serve as a proxy measurement of hazardous knowledge in biosecurity, cybersecurity, and chemical security. WMDP was developed by a consortium of academics and technical consultants, and was stringently filtered to eliminate sensitive information prior to public release. WMDP serves two roles: first, as an evaluation for hazardous knowledge in LLMs, and second, as a benchmark for unlearning methods to remove such hazardous knowledge. To guide progress on unlearning, we develop RMU, a state-of-the-art unlearning method based on controlling model representations. RMU reduces model performance on WMDP while maintaining general capabilities in areas such as biology and computer science, suggesting that unlearning may be a concrete path towards reducing malicious use from LLMs. We release our benchmark and code publicly at https://wmdp.ai
Computers and Society.comment: See the project page at https://wmdp.ai

Computers and Society.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
Computers and Society.summary: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
Computers and Society.comment: 10 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/AfifahK/bias-eval-construct-validity

Computers and Society.title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
Computers and Society.summary: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.

Digital Libraries.title: Can Large Language Models Estimate the Likely Technological Impact of Scientific Research? Evidence from Biotechnology
Digital Libraries.summary: This study provides large-scale empirical evidence about whether large language model (LLM)-based assessments of the likely technological impact of scientific publications are associated with their patent-based impact. Using Lens.org, we constructed a biotechnology dataset of 107,615 papers published between 1980 and 2015 with their patent citation counts. We used GPT-5-mini, Qwen-Flash, and DeepSeek-V3.2 to estimate papers technological impact and technology relevance, benchmarking model outputs against log-transformed patent-citation counts through correlation analysis, distributional alignment, and lift-over-random measures. The results show that LLMs extract meaningful signals associated with technological impact from scientific text, although there are substantial differences at the meso-level such as between research fields, journals, and countries. LLMs also outperform random selection in screening for papers with high observed patent impact. Overall, this study identifies the strengths, contexts, and limitations of LLM-based technological impact evaluation and highlights its potential to support large-scale screening for scientific work with downstream technological value.

Digital Libraries.title: How resampling method can help us: Improving the Delta model
Digital Libraries.summary: Delta has been successfully employed as an authorship attribution method in various contexts, although its effectiveness is not always perfect. Since it is based on the most frequent words, its results can be readily interpreted and explained in plain English. In this study, we propose improving its performance by applying a resampling method to the selected stylistic features. The results show that this approach increases the accuracy of the model while preserving the interpretability of its outcomes. However, the main drawback of the proposed technique is the additional computational time required to obtain more accurate results.

Digital Libraries.title: Is Sara Omar the true author of Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer)? Authorship attribution in Danish literature
Digital Libraries.summary: The bestseller Dødevaskeren (The Dead Washer) was published in 2017 under the name Sara Omar. A Danish colleague has suggested that the novel may have been written by another author, possibly Mads Peder Nordbo. To investigate this authorship question, four authorship attribution methods were applied, namely Delta, intertextual distance, Nearest Shrunken Centroids (NSC), and naïve Bayes. Using various parameter settings, these approaches consistently identify Nordbo's writing style in the doubtful novel, although the results do not provide conclusive evidence that he authored the novel in its entirety. In a second step, the novel was divided into non-overlapping segments of 5,000 tokens. Once again, Nordbo's style was identified in the majority of the segments. However, a small number of passages do not clearly support this conclusion and instead suggest the possible involvement of another, as yet unidentified, author, possibly Sara Omar herself.

Digital Libraries.title: Where Do Highly Cited Scientists Stand? A Multi-Dimensional Analysis of Positional Distribution in the Top 2% Ranking
Digital Libraries.summary: The Top 2% Scientists list is widely used. Yet current applications either only count the number of scientists in different units or criticize the list's validity as a measure of individual impact. We introduce positional enrichment, a scale-free framework that compares observed to expected counts across percentile bins on the list, revealing where a unit's scientists tend to sit along the list rather than how many it contributes. Applying positional enrichment to the 2026 single-year list, we show that countries, institutions, and research subfields each fall into a consistent pattern of three groups with Head-, Middle-, and Tail-enriched profiles. Subfield profiles are globally stable, whereas countries and institutions are heterogeneous across subfields. National and institutional differences are therefore compositional. Therefore, the reason of a country or institution sitting near the head of the list is unlikely its scientists performing better within the same subfields, while it holding more of the subfields that sit near the head. Academic age adds an independent dimension, with stronger enrichment toward the head after 25 years and exceptions in fast-moving subfields such as artificial intelligence. We show the ranking is not a flat ordering of individual influence but a subfield-organized stratification.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Product-Linear POSIX Parsing
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: POSIX regular-expression matching reports capture spans determined by the parse tree that its disambiguation rules select. Thompson's classical construction decides whether an expression $E$ matches a text $w$ in product-linear time, $O(|E|\,|w|)$. Whether the POSIX parse can also be computed in product-linear time has remained open since the rules were standardized in 1992. For instance, the algorithm of Okui and Suzuki takes $O(|E|^2|w|)$ time after precomputation. We give, to our knowledge, the first algorithm that computes the POSIX parse and all capture spans in product-linear total time, $O(|E|\,|w|)$. It uses $O(|E|+|w|)$ working space and supports full matching, longest-prefix matching, and leftmost-longest search. The algorithm scans the text backward and keeps one preferred continuation per traversal state. It implements POSIX selection with lists of end positions of the open subexpressions, which it compares and updates in constant time.

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: The Equational Theory of Rational String-to-String Functions
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: We give a sound and complete equational axiomatisation of the rational string-to-string functions, which can be seen as a transducer counterpart of the classical axiomatisations of regular languages by Salomaa [JACM'66], Krob [TCS'91], Bloom and Ésik [MSCS'93], and Kozen [IC'94]. The axioms are stated over a compositional, algebraic syntax for rational functions, namely the rational fragment of the syntax for regular functions introduced by Bojańczyk, Daviaud and Krishna [LICS'18]. The axiomatisation is finitary, as it consists of finitely many uniform families of axioms, each parameterised by the types involved. It is also purely equational: it consists only of equations, with no implication rules.
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.comment: Full version, with all proofs, of the POPL 2027 paper (Proc. ACM Program. Lang. 11, POPL, Article 101). 98 pages, 1 figure, 1 table. Lean formalisation: https://laxarchive.org/lax-149335/

Formal Languages and Automata Theory.title: Higher-Dimensional Automata in Geometric Logic
Formal Languages and Automata Theory.summary: What does the topos of a higher-dimensional automaton know about its infinite behaviour that its language does not? We write partial HDAs with an infinite run as models of a geometric theory over an intuitionistic metatheory with no choice. The topos of a machine is that of sheaves on its prefixes. The label word of a prefix records the shape and acceptance bit of each cell with the ipomset of each step. Under unique choice these words give a geometric morphism to the label topos of sheaves on label words, which thus records the shapes and acceptance bits that the Büchi language forgets. Machines sharing their Büchi language and their frames can differ over the label topos. The bouquet of two squares shares its frame and its Büchi language with the interleaved square; each accepted run of either reads the two events in parallel forever. Only the interleaved square has runs through cells of shape a, and the geometric sequent excluding such runs separates the two over the label topos. Over alphabets with decidable equality, finite rigid machines are unambiguous exactly when their label maps are inclusions of locales, and their equivalence over the label topos is decided whenever either is unambiguous. Equivalences of frames over the label topos transport points with their labels, and the invariants of fibres and of the language of points follow from this transport. On finite partial HDAs over alphabets with decidable equality, Muller and Büchi acceptance coincide exactly under a weak form of excluded middle.

Information Retrieval.title: Procedure Inference as Memory: Learning Recruiter Decision Procedures from OKF-Structured Episodes in Multi-Session Hiring Assistants
Information Retrieval.summary:
Multi-session hiring assistants must infer evolving recruiter preferences and decision patterns across projects and time. We introduce Open Knowledge Format (OKF)-indexed episodic memory to organize interactions and retrieve related events through their lineage. We also introduce Procedure Memory, which learns reusable decision procedures from these episodes through prompted reflection or reinforcement learning. We compare these approaches with no memory, full-history context, and conversation search, and evaluate Jev-class models for index navigation and GPT-5.6 Luna as a lower-cost alternative to GPT-5.4.
  In our evaluation, OKF-indexed retrieval achieves low-priority preference F1 scores of 0.93-0.95 at medium and high preference overlap between hiring projects. It significantly outperforms full-history context and conversation search in both settings, and no memory at high overlap, while using 69% fewer context tokens than full history. Procedure Memory reduces conversational turns by up to 39% relative to no memory. Qualitative and long-horizon evaluations provide evidence of temporal reasoning, with RL-learned procedures achieving 60% on both correct abstention and exact-field identification. Jev-class models improve conversational efficiency but more frequently miss temporally relevant evidence, highlighting the importance of evidence selection.
  On PersonaMem-v2, Procedure Memory with OKF retrieval achieves 50.2% accuracy versus 48.6% for full-history context and 29.0% for no memory, using 90.5% fewer reader input tokens than full history. GPT-5.6 Luna performs comparably to GPT-5.4 at lower cost. These findings highlight the value of structured episodic memory and learned decision procedures for efficient personalization and temporal reasoning.
Information Retrieval.comment: Includes supplementary appendices with experimental configurations, prompts, evaluation protocols, and learned procedure examples

Information Retrieval.title: KnowMe Paper Radar: Lightweight Discovery of Promising Papers in the Age of Autoresearch
Information Retrieval.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are pushing research toward semi-automation: ideas turn into preprints ever faster, and autoresearch pipelines add papers of uneven rigor. When a technique can be overtaken within months, citations arrive too late to tell which new papers deserve reading, so strong work goes unnoticed and newcomers lose their bearings. Yet from the day it appears, a preprint carries the track records of the people and institutions behind it. Established researchers guard their reputations and choose problems and collaborators with research taste, so their involvement tends to raise a paper's quality floor. Building on this signal, we present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight arXiv discovery tool that weights each paper's topical relevance by the reputation its authors and institutions stake on it. Author credit also diffuses by message passing along collaborations to surface rising stars, and institutions are profiled through the researchers they hold in each direction rather than by headcount. In a sealed test on 10,386 new papers, those with an identity-bound author were twice as likely to reach the top tenth of early citations. As its library grows into a scholarly knowledge graph that research agents can query through a command-line interface (CLI), KnowMe also offers a promising literature entry point for future autoresearch and recursive self-improvement (RSI).
Information Retrieval.comment: 60 pages, 29 figures and 37 tables. Project website: https://hackerchenzhuo.github.io/knowme-research-ai/en/ GitHub: https://github.com/hackerchenzhuo/knowme-research-ai

Information Retrieval.title: VulCPE: Context-Aware Cybersecurity Vulnerability Retrieval and Management
Information Retrieval.summary: The dynamic landscape of cybersecurity demands precise and scalable solutions for vulnerability management in heterogeneous systems, where configuration-specific vulnerabilities are often misidentified due to inconsistent data in databases like the National Vulnerability Database (NVD). Inaccurate Common Platform Enumeration (CPE) data in NVD further leads to false positives and incomplete vulnerability retrieval. Informed by our systematic analysis of CPE and CVEdeails data, revealing more than 50% vendor name inconsistencies, we propose VulCPE, a framework that standardizes data and models configuration dependencies using a unified CPE schema (uCPE), entity recognition, relation extraction, and graph-based modeling. VulCPE achieves superior retrieval precision (0.766) and coverage (0.926) over existing tools. VulCPE ensures precise, context-aware vulnerability management, enhancing cyber resilience.

Information Retrieval.title: Grounding User Preferences in Shared Multimodal Concepts for Recommendation
